annotationRationale: The problem tests choosing unordered cell sets and combining disjoint cases. The solution also justifies which final boards can actually occur under the stopping rule.

classificationReview.areaCheck: Counting & Probability is appropriate; no repair is needed.

review.questionCheck: The current statement and choices are consistent: Carl wins on move six, and the number of reachable final boards is 148, choice D. Random play affects probabilities, not which boards are possible. No figures or grading contradictions are present.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: No shared-bank methods were supplied. LIVE and AoPS give the same winning-line case split, which is retained. Another route would add little to this short count.
review.annotationCheck: Both assessed concepts are central: unordered selection of X cells and addition/multiplication across disjoint cases. Empty support and context lists are reasonable.
review.areaCheck: Counting & Probability is appropriate; no repair is needed.

methodReviews.mathCheck: The stated conditions are necessary and sufficient under the stopping rule. For each of six row/column O lines, exactly two of the 20 X selections win prematurely; for each diagonal, none do. Three O cells determine only one line, so there is no duplication. Thus 6(18)+2(20)=148.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Accurately identifies the equivalent LIVE and AoPS arguments as third-party sources and uses source-informed-original. The sufficiency proof and explanation of forbidden lines provide independent explanatory development.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: Clearly explains why final placements can replace move histories. The table entries, case totals, and absence of double counting are all justified.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: cnm_h239 precisely covers choosing three unordered cells; cnm_h232 covers multiplying within cases and adding the cases. Neither substitutes a broad topic for the decisive reasoning.
